segments.text: Unlike standard chatbots, like chat GBT or Claude, that primarily generate text to answer questions.
An AI agent is a computer program that takes independent action to finish a specific job for you.
Take this exact video course, for example.
We wanted a clean, custom layout for the lessons, but neither of us actually knows how to write the code to build one.
So, we used the built-in coding agents in chat GBT and Claude.
Instead of struggling with syntax, we just described the layout we wanted in plain English.
The agent took it from there.
It dug through our folders, found the right file, rewrote the underlying code,
and then ran a test to make sure the layout didn't break.
But it didn't publish it completely on its own.
We still had to review the final lesson closely to ensure the changes worked exactly as intended,
and more importantly, that it would be easy for our students to follow.
We were still the editors.
Writing code is just one specific use case.
Across dozens of different industries, tasks that used to require manual human effort are being handed off to these agents.
Programmers used to write code line by line, test it manually, and fix the bugs themselves.
Now a coding agent can execute all three of those phases autonomously.
Over in market research, professionals used to spend hours visiting competitors' websites one by one to log prices.
Today, an agent can automatically check those same products across dozens of sites
and compile a finished price comparison for a sales team.
For customer service, humans used to manually field phone calls and online chats.
Now an agent can handle both simultaneously.
If a customer asks for a package update, the agent queries the order database,
checks the tracking, and sends the response.
And in standard office work, the routine of copying sales figures into spreadsheets
to build weekly presentation slides is changing.
An agent can update those numbers and prepare the team slide deck on its own.
In all of these fields, the software is taking large volumes of routine,
time-consuming busy work, completely off people's plates.
But stripping away all that busy work naturally raises a massive question.
If agents can do much of the work that makes up a job,
what happens to the people doing that job today?
So how does an agent actually do the work once you hand it off?
Step one is the goal.
You, the human operator, dictate the exact outcome you want to achieve.
Step two is the plan.
The agent takes your macro goal and dissects it into a sequence of executable microsteps.
Step three is act.
The agent selects the appropriate digital tool and executes the next step in its sequence.
Then comes the check.
The agent evaluates its own output, looking at the result to see if it actually met your original objective.
If the check fails, the agent doesn't stop and wait for you to prompt it again.
It automatically loops back to the planning phase, adjusting its approach to try again.
The agent has the autonomy to finish a task, retry a failed step, or ask for help,
but you are still the one setting the parameters and judging the final success.
Agents do the work, but the name on it is yours.
You ask, it acts, you make it better.
